title: The pilgrims turned back
hook: fourteen hundred set out as pilgrims for Mecca; the Prophet's camel kneels and won't go on, and they are stopped at the well of Hudaybiyyah (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wind, and Hudhayfah lowering his bow in the enemy camp. Your line was: the wind came.

This time they aren't marching to a battle. They're going on pilgrimage. Sahih al-Bukhari describes them setting out from Medina with their sacrificial animals garlanded and marked, and entering the state of ihram, the pilgrim's state, on the road. Al-Bara, who was there, says they were fourteen hundred. The goal is the Ka'bah, the house they have faced in prayer from far away. And then, close to Mecca, the Prophet's camel kneels down in the road and won't get up. Today: the pilgrims turned back.
screen: `NOT A BATTLE: A PILGRIMAGE.` → `ANIMALS GARLANDED, PILGRIMS IN IHRAM.` → `THE CAMEL KNEELS.`

segments.voice: The camel's name is al-Qaswa, and in Bukhari's long report the people around her start saying: al-Qaswa has turned stubborn. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ answers: she hasn't, that isn't her nature. She has been held back by the One who held back the elephant: a reference to Surah al-Fil, the army with the elephant that never reached the Ka'bah. A stopped animal, and he reads it as a sign: not this way, not by force. Then he says what sets the tone for everything after: by the One in whose hand is my soul, if they ask me for any plan that honors what Allah has made sacred, I will grant it. He turns the camel and they camp at Hudaybiyyah, at the edge of the sacred land, by a well with very little water. Al-Bara tells what happened there. They drew the well until it was dry. The Prophet sat at its edge, asked for some water, rinsed his mouth, made a supplication, and poured it back into the well. After a while, he says, the well gave enough for them and their animals. So here they are: pilgrims in ihram, water in the well, and a closed door ahead. The Meccans will not let them in. A pledge, a treaty and an argument over a single word are coming. Today is only the stopping. Much of this week has been about stopping: archers who should have stayed, defenders who held their ground, a man who held his arrow. And now a whole caravan, halted at the edge.
screen: `AL-QASWA KNEELS.` · `HELD BACK BY THE ONE WHO HELD BACK THE ELEPHANT.` · `A DRY WELL AT HUDAYBIYYAH.` · `A CLOSED DOOR AHEAD.` · then, large: `STOPPED AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one door that's closed to you right now, a job that went to someone else, a plan the world said no to, and picture yourself at its edge, ready, with your hand resting on it instead of pushing. Then turn around and look for the well: what's here, where you are, that you haven't drawn from yet. If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you the well.
Hudaybiyyah, the well at the edge of the sacred land where the pilgrim caravan, in ihram for the Ka'bah, was stopped. Today's word.
Your line: stopped at the edge. The camel knelt, and he read it as a sign. That's day seven hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims setting out for hajj or umrah enter ihram at set points on the road, as the pilgrims of Hudaybiyyah did, and the story of the journey is taught in sirah classes.

read it as a sign, and turn aside.

original.note: Arabic: Hudaybiyyah, the name of the place and its well at the edge of the sacred land near Mecca.

trapdoor: what you thought: a trip that failed.
what it means: pilgrims stopped at the edge, reading the stop as a sign rather than forcing the door.
what a scholar hears: al-Qaswa and the elephant in Bukhari 2731, al-Bara's well in Bukhari 4150, and the garlanded animals.

chat.says: When his camel knelt and wouldn't go on, how did the Prophet take it?
options: As a sign: held back, like the elephant, so not by force.
As a stubborn animal that needed a firmer hand to move.
As a sign to fight his way into Mecca the next morning.
chat.meaning: She has been held back by the One who held back the elephant, he said, and he offered any plan that honors what Allah made sacred.

ihram.meaning: the pilgrim's sacred state, entered on the road

Hudaybiyyah.meaning: a place and well at the edge of the sacred land

Ka'bah.meaning: the house in Mecca that Muslims face in prayer

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731–2732 (the garlanded animals and ihram; al-Qaswa kneels; held back by the One who held back the elephant; 'any plan that honors what Allah has made sacred')
Sahih al-Bukhari 4150 (al-Bara: fourteen hundred at Hudaybiyyah; the well drawn dry and filled again)
Qur'an 105 (Surah al-Fil: the army of the elephant)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm Bukhari 2731–2732 and 4150 and the details drawn from them.
The number fourteen hundred is from al-Bara in Bukhari 4150 (other reports in Bukhari give slightly different numbers); confirm.
Bukhari 2731 has a different telling of the well (an arrow placed in it); the script follows al-Bara's version in 4150. A Keeper may wish to mention both.
'At the edge of the sacred land' summarizes the reports' and commentators' placement of Hudaybiyyah; confirm.

Editor: the practice no longer offers 'hasbiyallah', which repeated day 783's 'hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil' the day before; it now invites asking Allah, in general terms, to show the well. Cut 'close enough to Mecca to almost see it' (not in the cited reports) and 'pilgrims in white' became 'pilgrims in ihram'.
Day 784 is a week end; the end of the teach looks back at days 779–783.
Year 2 day 580 covered the treaty's terms and Surah al-Fath; this day covers only the stopping, leaving the pledge (785) and the treaty's title (786) to the next days.
Audit: week look-back said the Uhud defenders 'stood still'; they fought, so now 'held their ground'.
Job 2: the teach's look-ahead ('what comes next, this path will tell over the coming days') and the week look-back kept, shortened.
